videos.title: Things I Wish I knew Before Buying a VW TDI
videos.transcript_text:
This video will be about TDI from The Mk3 to the 
Mk7. If you want to learn specifically about the
MK6 cars check out my Mk6 TDI buyer's guide as 
well. There will be some overlap if you watch
both, but both videos will have extra information 
you might not get from the other. For some context
I've owned my TDI since 130,000 miles, it's 
currently at 192,000. I've done a lot of reading
before and after buying. This is a passion of mine 
and I'm always eager to learn something new about
these engines. I've also helped to maintain 
and repair various other TDI owned by friends
and family. To start off let's talk about one of 
the biggest reasons people buy TDIs. Real world
fuel economy. By and large a TDI will get better 
fuel economy than the EPA estimates. The EPA tests
aren't ideal conditions for TDI fuel economy. The 
way they test these cars is standardized instead
of individualized per car. This is part of the 
reason why some cars get much less and others
much more than the EPA estimates. The dieselgate 
cars especially get more as the were tested with
the clean cheat which resulted in less power 
and worse MPG. All TDI cars seem to follow this
sort of trend though, willing you're able to 
adapt your driving habits. In my MK6 TDI Golf,
with a manual transmission, the best tank I've 
gotten is 56 MPG, the worst I've gotten is 42.
The 42 MPG tank was a lot of spirited driving and 
idling. Even when I pushed this car through some
back roads with my buddies for an afternoon, 
I returned 40 MPG on the trip and 45 from the
tank when I filled up later in the week. And 
the second item TDI buyers care about most,
reliability. This car has never skipped a beat. 
I have had one issue, a busted sway bar end link
that caused a clunk. 20 minutes and $50 to replace 
both sides, back in business, no more clunk! I've
only done preventative maintenance, one set of 
brakes, and the sway bar end links. It's never
let me down, never been stuck on the side of 
the road. There was one issue before I hit the
infamous pothole though. I did go through one full 
emission system under warranty. My driving habits
were the cause though, a lot of short trips and 
too much idling at the time. If you take longer
trips and don't idle too long I don't think the 
emissions components are actually too problematic.
There are others that would disagree and there 
are outlier examples on both sides, but this was
my experience with a fixed dieselgate car. Power 
add-ons. The default answer to power out of a TDI
is a pothole and tune. Though you can get a Malone 
tune without deletes and add that on later, kerma
also offers intact emissions tuning but they do 
not offer a delete tune to upgrade to. Because of
this reason I would stick with Malone for tuning 
unless you're 100% certain you'll be keeping the
emission system for the life of the vehicle. For 
other items, there are some dyo results that show
a high flow intake does have small advantages, 
but there is a large debate about this on various
forums and Facebook groups. I'll link the dyno 
results in the description. I personally do have
an aftermarket intake on my car, but I understand 
it's mostly a difference in sound and for me
personally I wanted to remove the airbox since 
the screws had rusted and stripped twice on me
already. Finding diesel fuel. I've never had an 
issue finding a station that offers diesel. At
most I see one station that doesn't offer it and 
the next does. That's been my experience driving
around in the midwest at least. As far as where 
to fill up if you have options or can plan it out,
I personally try to go to stations truckers go 
to, that ensures they have a fresh batch which
can also help the various components of the 
fuel system which is especially important on
the common rail cars with high pressure fuel 
pumps. Fuel additives, I personally run fuel
additives in my car it's relatively cheap piece 
of mind. I use power service and store it in these
LiquiMoly diesel additive bottles to transport 
it. Power service bottles leak and when they leak,
they smell horrible and stain whatever they touch. 
The LiquiMoly bottles haven't leaked on me yet
and it's easy to carry one tank worth of fluid. I 
simply use the power service calculator to figure
out roughly how much to fill the LiquiMoly bottle 
and use it that way. Oil, the oil specifications
on these cars are pretty easy to find and follow. 
Here are some examples on screen. The only outlier
that needs mentioning is the pump deuse 505.01 
oil. There are some 5W30 oils with this oil cert,
but the general consensus is that running the 5w40 
will protect the camshaft better. Common failures,
most common failures on all of these are emissions 
components EGRs, DPFs, adblue systems. The pothole
is equally aimed at reliability as it is at 
power or fuel economy gains. The pump duese
engines have the aformentioned camshaft issues 
when improperly oiled the ALH has issues with
glowplug harnesses. The pump duese can get 
a colt camshaft upgrade so you never have to
think about it again and the glowplug harness 
on an ALHi s a little over $100 for OEM. Other
items are going to be chassis related instead of 
engine related so I'll refrain from going deeper.
Automatic transmissions the automatics on the 
alh cars is is the 01m fourspeed with the mark
3i is using a very similar four-speed Auto being 
a fourspeed these aren't going to get great fuel
economy and they aren't known for being robust 
I've personally had to replace the harness and
solenoids on my brother's 2.0 markv wagon that is 
equipped with the same transmission and while it's
not the worst job in the world it's certainly not 
fun the later marvs with the pump Deuce come with
a 5-speed Tiptronic automatic which are better but 
still widely disregarded because they simply won't
last as long as the engine will the Dual clutch 
or DSG transmissions on the mark 5 through the
Mark 7 cars are quite reliable if you keep up on 
maintenance you should be doing a DSG fluid and
filter change every 40,000 mil on these otherwise 
you risk a lot of problems I would recommend 40
to 60,000 Mi fluid and filter intervals on 
any automatic transmission and every 60 to
80k on manuals but for the Dual clutch GE boxes 
especially every 40K manual transmissions while
these Transmissions will typically last the life 
of the vehicle there are reports of DMF failure a
symptom of this would be chattering at idle and 
low speeds this is most often caused by abusive
driving particularly not downshifting to pass 
and flooring it in a high gear if you do need to
replace the DMF put in an upgraded DMF upgraded 
clutch and replace the slave cylinder same goes
for if you need to replace the slave cylinder 
because on a mark 5 through Mark 7 manual car
the slave cylinder is unfortunately internal on 
those Transmissions so to swap it out you'll have
to drop the whole transmission if at any point you 
have to drop the transmission I would recommend
upgrading if you do begin to go down this Rabbit 
Hole you might find mentions of a single Mass
flywheel upgrade these are fine on early Mark 
5 transmissions and on Mark 4S but do not use a
single Mass flywheel on a Mark 6 or Mark 7 this is 
a highly debated topic but to add some clarity the
markv and early Mark 5 use brass synchros they can 
hold up to a single Mass flywheel the Mark 6 and
seven cars use steel synchros and can be destroyed 
with a single Mass flywheel as I mentioned in the
automatic transmission segment I would recommend 
doing fluid and filter changes on these every 60
to 80,000 mil as peace of mind I plan for this 
to be my forever car so I have no issue going
above and beyond to keep it in tiptop shape TDI 
stigma I have run into some people that want to
talk about the emission Scandal respectfully or 
disrespectfully I proudly present the dieselgate
topic on my car it's no secret but when I talk 
with someone who is less than happy with what
they think the TDI has done to the planet I do my 
best to rationalize things with them bringing up
the real world numbers such as a Modern Diesel is 
cleaner than an older gasoline car and unless I
was going to step into a car payment again which 
I have no intention of doing I'd be replacing my
TDI with an old gas car which would actually 
be worse for the environment mile per mile and
that's discounting a handful of things Parts 
aren't carbon neutral to replace so far engine
wise I've had to replace nothing besides filters 
and oil even Spark plugs and ignition coils have
some carbon emissions when being produced and 
transported two wear items that simply aren't
present on a diesel motor tires are actually 
the biggest source of Emissions on road cars
to the tune of about 2,000 times compared to 
the tailpipe of the car the actual amount of
pollution caused by motorists is about 15% of 
the world's total greenhouse gases this isn't
a small amount but whatever my share is there 
are much bigger things at play besides what I
drive and how I drive a dog has a larger carbon 
footprint than a full-size truck year to year but
you'd never shout about saving the trees if you 
saw me walking my dog a TDI isn't for everyone
maybe you still can't get past the stigma maybe 
you do run a lot of short trips and can't poth
hole it but for those it does make sense for you 
won't find a better daily driver or road trip car

a fourspeed these aren't going to get great fuel

So the EA288, the 2 liter TDI diesel,
takes over from the EA 189, which let's
face it, was dogged with problems. The
Volkswagen Group had done their best to
improve things over the years. So the
question is, how much better is the
EA288? We're not going to go quite as
far as the 2018 revision of this engine,
which is referred to as the EVO, which
again was a major leap forward. In terms
of Volkswagen diesel engines, the EA288
is a considerably better engine than its
4Erunners. So, in this video, we're just
going to highlight some of the common
things that crop up. Now, don't think of
these as significant faults. The
previous engines, the older you went,
you seem to have more and more problems
and issues creeping up. So, some of
these problems only really manifest
themselves when you get up to 150,000,
200,000 miles. So, for most drivers,
they would consider these as reliable
engines with no problems whatsoever. But
at this point in time, you may well be
buying one that's got a higher mileage.
So, this video really serves as
highlighting the things you need to look
out for when you're looking to buy one
of these amazing 2 L TDI engines.
[Music]
It's fair to say that Volkswagen have
had a few issues over the years with
their 2 L TDI engine, as have many other
manufacturers. Now, Volkswagen often
push the envelope. They're innovators
when it comes to designing engines and
trying out new technology. So, they're
often first to the market or they
massproduce engines that other car
manufacturers are still developing in
the background. So, it's nice to have
this technology coming out so quickly,
but often there are problems that
manifest themselves as the engines start
to get older. So thankfully they've
looked back at the common problems that
happen with the older engines and
they've engineered out a lot of these
faults and issues on the EA288. So
there's just a few things I want to flag
up as things to look out for potential
problems. Now firstly the EA288 like all
diesel engines has a DPF, a diesel
particulate filter. If you do short
journeys, you don't warm it up and you
don't go through the proper heat
generation cycles, you will get a
problem with that. That's a fact of life
of having a diesel particulate filter on
an engine. So the design of the diesel
particulate filters, the positioning in
this is significantly better in the
previous engines. So it's not dogged
with as much of a bad reputation as its
forerunners, but it does require you to
be aware that you've got a DPF filter
and adjust your driving style
accordingly. The previous engines were
dogged in the dieselgate emissions
scandal where Volkswagen cheated the
emissions regulations with a software
defeat that detected test conditions and
backed everything off so the car would
meet emissions. So there's allegations
again against the early versions of the
EA288 engine still forming part of this
emissions scandal. So it'll be
interesting to see how the courts deal
with this and how Volkswagen handle
these particular allegations. You can't
assume that this EA288 is completely
free of those diesel allegations because
there are still some rumors and some
pending investigations going on out
there. So, if you've got some updates on
that, please let us know in the comments
how that's gone. So, having direct
injection and just the way the engine
works, it's got an EGR valve and there's
a positive crankase ventilation system.
All of these add up to the possibility
of having carbon building up on the
intake. So most people will just
consider this as a a routine thing. Now
you tend to accept that this will happen
on modern engines and just get a clean
done on the intake every 50,000 to
70,000 mi. So that's really part of
routine maintenance. Changing your spark
plugs in a gasoline or petrol engine is
not really considered a problem or a
fault. It's just something you have to
do. So people are starting to feel the
same way about the carbon buildup
problems. Now, the carbon buildup speed
is much reduced on these EA288 engines.
We're doing another video that's going
to be out soon that's just discussing
some of the revisions that Volkswagen
have made to improve this problem, but I
can't dogmatically say that the EA288
will have no intake problems because
it's direct injection and it's got all
those pollution control systems. So,
there is going to be a risk of having
carbon building up on those intake. But,
it's much slower. It's much improved and
Volkswagen have done a pretty good job
in mitigating this issue as the mileage
starts to creep up. You're starting to
see problems with the fuel injectors.
Now, bear in mind that these injectors
are working under really high pressures.
This is a modern turbo diesel engine.
It's been designed to meet modern
emissions regulations. It gives a
phenomenal amount of performance to you
as a driver. So, those injectors are
working pretty hard. So, these aren't
the failures that just happen randomly
at low mileages. As the injectors start
to age, they will start to deteriorate.
So, injector replacement is quite
expensive. Some firms are offering
replacements and reconditioned unit.
There's also a whole host of aftermarket
options that you can go for if you
wanted to upgrade the fuel injectors.
So, that's probably something worth
thinking about if you've got a tuning
project and you want to get a little bit
more performance out of your engine.
But, keep an eye on the injectors. If
you're starting to have power problems
or power issues and the mileage is
creeping up, it could well be those old
injectors. is starting to fail and
starting to play up. So, get those
investigated and checked out. So, these
engines use a fairly complex cooling
system. The the variable flow water pump
is often subject to failure. Again, this
isn't something that just happens
randomly on low mileages. So, we're not
talking about an inherent defect here,
but these water pumps can fail at higher
mileages. So things to look out for on
the water pumps is abnormal noises,
vibrations, anything that would indicate
maybe there's friction going on inside
the water pump and random coolant
temperature drops or peaks and a car not
warming up properly or a car not cooling
down when it's being run particularly
hot. So get a feel for how the baseline
is on these engines and if you notice
anything out of the norm, get the water
pump investigated. That's most likely
going to be the area where you start to
see problems developing. So, the exhaust
gas recirculation system is again fairly
complex in the EA288. They've done it to
meet the emissions regulations. Um, it
generally only really kicks in at low
RPMs during the warm-up phases. At high
RPM driving under full load, the EGR
system is pretty much shut off. So, it's
not something that's going to impact
your performance adversely, but it is
circulating those exhaust gases. It goes
through a cooler before it goes into the
intake. And it's actually in that cooler
where you start to see it clogging up
and blocking up. So again, keep an eye
on that. If you have a high mileage
version of this engine, get the EGR
cooler system stripped down and cleaned
out if you suspect there's a problem
going on in this area. You may well
start to have rough running problems.
The emissions may start to creep up.
There may be warning lights coming on
the dashboard and you may be throwing
error code. Each of those things could
indicate that it's the EGR cooler that's
starting to play up. So turbos on these
engines are pretty good. Most people we
speak to say they last to about 150,000
mi, which is reasonably good in a modern
engine. And at that sort of mileage, you
may well start to think about upgrading
it, replacing it with a better unit and
turning this car into a project car
where you renew it as much as you can,
but you do it to a much higher
performance level just to take that to
the next level. And the dual mass
flywheel, like any dual mass flywheel,
it's taking a lot of stress and
vibration out of the engine. There's two
plates. There's a spring mechanism
connecting those two plates together.
And it does take its toll. Again, this
is something that tends to affect the
engines well over 150,000 mi. People
have said to us about 200, 220,000 mi,
you start to get DMF failure. So, if you
notice noises coming from the
transmission, rough running, that could
all be a sign that the DMF is starting
to break apart or starting to fail. So,
get that addressed early on. if if you
leave it too long, you can start to run
up some pretty serious repair bills and
have other problems developing in the

It's a great engine. There's a few

interesting. Thanks for watching.

videos.title: Volkswagen’s 1.5 TSI engine: Common problems and advantages
videos.transcript_text:
The 1.5 TSI engine belongs to the EA211 
family, and it was first introduced in
2014. The company has been using these 
engines in almost all kinds of models,
starting with the Polo and up to the Passat, 
Touran, or even Arteon. Also, Audi, Seat,
and Skoda models have been using this engine 
heavily, and now it’s one of the most widespread
modern-generation engines in Volkswagen’s lineup.
Even though the TSI type of engines got a lot of
hatred when they first appeared about 20 years 
ago, now they are considered quite reliable,
very economical, efficient, and basically 
non-problematic engines. The 1.5 TSI is also
available as the mild-hybrid engine, 1.5 eTSI, 
and it utilizes the same base, so everything in
this video will cover that hybrid version, too.
Please keep in mind that I will focus on common
problems, so the video may seem a little 
negative. But I personally think that the
1.5 TSI engine is quite good and only has several 
drawbacks that owners just need to know about.
First of all, starting from the very beginning 
of its life and up to model year 2024,
these engines had a very disturbing feature known 
as the kangaroo effect. It appeared to torture
owners of cars with manual transmissions. Once 
you start driving in the first gear, the engine
may suddenly lower RPMs and nearly stall, but then 
everything comes back to normal. It seems like you
are a bad driver, and it may be quite embarrassing 
at times. Fortunately, the most recent updates
seem to have finally fixed this issue. But 
if you still experience it, try releasing
the clutch pedal completely before you start 
pressing the gas pedal. This should help a lot.
The compression ratio of 12.5 to 1 is not typical 
for petrol engines, so I believe using low-octane
fuel is not an option. European classification 
octane number 95 or higher is recommended by
the manufacturer, but owners admit that 98 
petrol works well, while anything lower than
that may cause slight knocking and loss of power.
Also, these engines are able to deactivate two of
the cylinders, shifting one of the camshafts to 
another position. The system looks quite good,
but experts still don’t know if it’s 
going to last long enough. For now,
there haven’t been any serious problems 
with this cylinder deactivation system, so I
believe it’s never going to be a serious problem.
The engine uses a variable geometry turbocharger,
which is also not that typical for petrol 
engines. And I know about some cases when
these turbos failed and required replacement, 
but I wouldn’t say the problem is very common.
The engine is equipped with the timing belt, and 
the service requirements are very tangled. In the
first generation of the 1.5 TSI engine, Volkswagen 
recommended cambelt replacement once every 5 years
or 140,000 miles or 225,000 kilometers. After 
updates in 2023, the engine has two types of
recommendations: no requirements for belt 
replacement or changing once every 15 years
or 180,000 miles, 300,000 kilometers. Basically, 
the belt is considered for the entire lifespan
of the engine, but I would replace it at 150K 
miles anyway if I wanted to drive this car for
long enough. This is a simple dry belt system, 
but it’s not very cheap to replace, and there
is no evidence that the belt is problematic, 
so no need to replace it once every 5 years.
Other than that, there is a common issue of oil 
consumption after the engine hits 100,000 miles
or 150,000 kilometers. So, high-mileage engines 
will need to be checked for oil level regularly.
I can tell you that even though I’m not 
that into Volkswagen cars and technologies,
this 1.5 TSI engine seems to be a great machine. 
The company learned its lessons with the early
1.4 TSI mistakes and made a significantly 
better engine. I hope this video was helpful,
and I also hope that you will write in the 
comments about your experience with these engines.

videos.title: VW Golf GTD Review - after 8 years is it still any good?
videos.transcript_text:
Can you beat the VW Golf? It’s a tricky one 
- I’m no VW expert, but I think the Golf is a
pretty good all-rounder and after 8 years owning 
this Golf GTD here’s the ultimate long term test!
There is also one thing I am absolutely gutted 
about not ordering on this car from new though,
which I’ll get to later on in this video.
So, this is the MK7 Golf 2ltr GTD 184bhp, which 
as I have mentioned, I have owned for 8 years
now and covered approximately 70,000 miles and 
although it’s not the flashiest car on the road,
I think it has that quiet ‘you know I 
have kudos’ status out there on the roads.
Some say the Mk7 Golf is the last proper Golf, 
what do you think - let me know in the comments
below.
I’ve created this video to show you what I’ve 
enjoyed about this car over the years and maybe
some of the things I haven’t enjoyed quite 
so much. Also, I thought watching this may
be useful for anyone thinking about buying 
a used Golf GTD at some point in the future?
By the way, it would be amazing for me if you 
wouldn’t mind subscribing and liking and I’ll keep
putting together the best content I can for you.
CONTENT
So, back in 2015 I paid around £25,000 pounds 
-that’s approx $31,000 USD for this car. Although
I was tempted to order some factory options at 
the time, I decided to stick to the standard spec,
which was plenty for me, or so I thought - anyway… 
the only extra cost was adding the metallic paint
option.
And I opted for Carbon Steel Metallic which 
I think is a beautiful colour for this car.
It’s a rich dark grey/graphite tonne. 
And with this being a GTD it sets off
the sportier highlights of this model, 
such as the deeper front bumper,
where you can just see the cornering lights, 
the flared sills and at the rear the colour
blends in nicely with the chunky rear bumper, 
smoked rear light lenses and twin tailpipes.
The wheels are the standard 18” Nogaro
alloys with low profile tyres. I have Michelin 
tyres fitted. I’ve had Bridgestone in the past,
but I find these Michelin’s create less road 
noise and handle the wet weather really well.
I love the look of the Nogaro alloys, but 
if I’m honest I also know I don’t have to
put much effort into cleaning them if I 
am feeling lazy, as they’re mainly black.
One downside to the low-profile tyres though,
especially on UK roads is that 
horrible ‘bang’ when you hit a pothole.
Fortunately, I’ve been lucky 
and only had to replace 1 tyre,
but every time you hit a pothole with 
these wheels it doesn’t feel or sound
good at all!
The bi-xenon headlamps are pretty cool too, super 
bright and the auto headlights are very handy.
I’ve never kept a car for this long and I think it 
may be because although this car is 8 years old,
it still has some pretty good spec such as 
a tyre pressure sensor, sat nav, touchscreen
display as well as parking sensors front and rear 
and adaptive cruise control. More on what I think
of the ACC later.
Another handy thing is that I like the way I 
can check I have locked my car from a distance.
By setting the mirrors to the auto fold function 
they will fold and unfold when the car is locked
and unlocked. There’s no audible beep so this is 
a simple visual indication that you’ve locked your
car and is very useful.
Inside you’re met with the GTD trim, classic 
VW Golf checked upholstery with sports seats,
and upgraded standard GTD spec 
such as a leather steering wheel.
The steering wheel has a great feel, but be 
careful – it scuffs easily as you can see.
I didn’t opt for leather seats this time 
and I’m pretty pleased with that choice
now after the recent hot summers. As 
you can see, I’ve got heated seats,
which came as part of the standard Winter 
Pack at the time. Super nice in the winter.
The on board computer is very handy and I use
it’s functions all the time. An example is that 
it shows instant and long term miles per gallon
averages. I average about 52 miles per gallon 
and up to 59 miles per gallon on long runs.
The touchscreen display does what it says on

The seventh-generation golf GTI was built
on the MQB platform that is ubiquitous across
the Volkswagen Group and was revealed in Berlin,
Germany on September the 4th of 2012.
The GTI began deliveries in 2013 and all models
are Euro 6 emissions compliant.
Throughout
Its production the Golf GTI was only offered
with a third generation 2-litre four-cylinder
engine, coded EA888.
A three and five door variant were available
at launch for some markets, and continued
late into the life of the Golf GTI however
for some markets the three door was dropped
after a facelift in 2017, while others had
a limited supply or special editions that
remained in three-door.
By the end of production, the three-door was
gone and in the eight generation all Golf
models are now five-door only.
The facelift model, commonly referred to as
the MK7.5 GTI was seen as a new Golf by VW,
but most informally referred to it as a facelifted
MK7.5 and it has won a large enthusiast following
with many believing the 7.5 gen is the peak
of the Volkswagen Golf GTI as the eighth generation
moved to a new styling and interior design
although it stuck with the same platform.
There are many changes to the MK7.5 but they
are easily identified by a digital dash and
larger infotainment screen and revised exterior
styling.
The GTI was sold with a variety of power outputs
depending on options or special edition models.
The base GTI made 217bhp, with the most powerful
creating 306bhp, but we’ll come onto these
further on in the video.
During the production of the Volkswagen Golf
a variety of version aside from the standard
model were offered including an optional Performance
Pack which is highly desirable on the used
market.
There was also special edition models including
the 2016 GTI Club sport that was sold with
optional Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 tires
and a limited slip differential.
This was followed by the GTI Clubsport S in
the same year, which was a three door only
edition with more power and uprated suspension
and subframe compared to the regular Clubsport
model, a total of 400 were produced.
There was also a TCR model released in 2019.
Some markets were also offered a ‘rabbit
edition’ in 2019 that featured styling tweaks
and a rabbit logo.
First up in our guide are the areas you should
look out for across the life of the seventh
generation Golf GTI, as ever our lists are
non-exhaustive and so if you know of any common
issue that we have missed please add them
to the comments below.
First up there is a note for owners and potential
buyers of manual transmission models that
the clutch is generally considered at its
power limit from the factory, if you have
any intent on tuning it will likely reduce
the service life of the clutch and an uprated
model should be considered to handle the additional
power.
Vehciles equipped with a sunroof may have
had the seal either wrongly fitted or an inadequately
sized part may have been fitted from factory.
Several service bulletins and recall notices
should have resolved effected models, however
it is worth check around the seal on a used
example.
Electrical damage has occurred on some vehicles
where the issue has not been resolved
Washer fluid sensors are susceptible to failure
if the wrong fluid is used due to their design.
If you get see and engine management light
that points to washer fluid this is the most
likely cause.
Parcel shelf clips are susceptible to breaking
if put under too much stress while load carrying.
They can also become damaged without completely
breaking which will cause a rattle.
Water ingress into the passenger footwell
has been reported caused by a crack in the
mounting bracket for the door speaker.
Look carefully for any signs of discolored
carpet or damp patches on the passenger side
when viewing a vehicle.
If you experience poor heater performance
or the fan speed is weak on all setting then
the blower motor has likely failed.
Code B10BE will show up on diagnostic equipment
if this is the case.
If this issue only arises when using the air
conditioning and is accompanied by a noise
in the engine bay then the problem is with
the air conditioning solenoid valve.
Any clunking sound from the front end that
is not caused by worn dampers or bushings
is likely from the subframe bolts.
When looking to buy a vehicle make sure the
latch and release cable for the bonnet release
is operable without a large amount of effort.
If so the mechanisms is under additional stress
and likely to fail.
A broken bonnet release cable is a common
issue across the 7th generation Golf, but
as we highlight in all our guides, for an
issue to be classed as common it is usually
between 1-5% of production vehicles.
Finally the oil pan is plastic, this in itself
shouldn’t be much of a problem although
heat cycling the pan has caused a small number
of owners to report the need for replacement.
It was difficult to identify whether these
were just meticulous owners that had noticed
a fractional difference or oil pans on the
edge of failure, however the drain plug is
also plastic and must be replaced after every
oil change rather than reused.
Expect oil leaks if the plastic plug is reused.
Next up are the common faults with the engine,
and as a single unit is used we will start
by mentioning issues likely to impact all
power output models, and then specify and
particular issues.
First up though a reminder that if you want
more from the Miles Driven we have a website
and a podcast, and if you are enjoying the
video then a like really does make a huge
difference the discoverability of videos on
youtube.
As ever we appreciate every subscriber to
our channel
The 2.0-litre third generation EA888 engine
found in the Golf GTI is a cast iron block
with aluminum head with a bore of 82.5mm and
a stroke of 92.8mm for a total displacement
of 1984cc.
Fuel consumption varies slightly depending
on specification and age but official figures
hover between 43.7mpg and 47.1mpg.
One of the reasons for this relatively low
fuel consumption is that the third generation
EA888 motor adds water-cooling to the exhaust
manifold speed up the time it takes to warm
up from a cold start and then to maintain
temperatures while operating.
The early Golf GTI produces 217bhp, with the
performance pack boosting this to 227bhp.
The performance pack also adds a limited slip
differential named VAQ along with uprated
brakes.
The Clubsport model produced 306bhp becoming
the most powerful Golf GTI, a record that
the late TCR model was unable to beat due
to the additional exhaust restrictions introduced
in 2018, the TCR produced 286bhp.
First up you should note that PCV failure
is one of the more common issues found on
the EA888 engine and a common side effect
with be the failure of the rear main seal,
causing an oil leak.
Deterioration of the plastic housing for the
thermostat is one of the most common areas
for coolant loss.
If you can smell coolant but struggle to visually
see a leak then this is likely culprit.
The other likely cause is a failing or failed
water pump.
Turbo charger failure is a known fault of
models fitted with the 06K 145 702N unit fitted
in many 2015to 2017 models.
A revision to the design was made after this
date and so if the unit fitted to your car
ends 722 then the vehicle was either fitted
from factory with the updated unit or has
been replaced at some point in the vehicles
history.
The seal from turbo to manifold seems to be
the weak spot and the reason for the 702N
turbo failures.
Fault codes P0300, P0301, P0302, P0303, P0304
are all likely signs of an ignition coil pack
failure.
A side note is that the end number relates
to each cylinder, so for example the P0303
would be an issue detected in cylinder number
three.
The code ending zero is a multiple cylinder
misfire.
Other signs of this failure are poor engine
running and rough idle.
Carbon build up on valves is a side effect
of the injection system on these engines.
Owners generally believe every 60,000 miles
the valves need to manually cleaned.
Some believe walnut blasting is better than
sand blasting , there are other types of media
that can also be used.
If you believe one way or another is better
let us known in the comments.
Some owners running premium fuel report better
longevity and less carbon build up but this
point becomes contentious with others believing
use of additives on a regular basis better,
let us know your thoughts in the comments.
Finally, some cars produced for model year
2015 and 2016 had a recall code 20Y6 to replace
a pump in the fuel tank for the EVAP system.
Clogged charcoal cannisters are a sign of
failure and the total number of vehicles recalled
for this issue exceeded 100,000.
If we’ve missed any other common faults
please let us know to help in the comments
to help owners and potential buyers.
For our picks we would suggest those with
a lower budget purchase a good condition early
standard model and then improve the vehicle
rather than limiting themselves to one with
the upgraded performance pack as these demand
a premium and so better condition standard
models will likely be a better buy unless
you find a great deal.
If shopping with a higher budget go for the
mk7.5 wherever possible.
If a three door works for your needs that
is what we would go for however a five door
does add practicality.
